about: Spark / Build / Invent challenges per station. prompt is copy-ready with [brackets] to fill in. hints are revealed one at a time: nudge, model, worked example.

challenges.title: Three-turn story
challenges.brief: Ask Claude for a short story, then make it better in three follow-up turns instead of starting over.
challenges.prompt: Write a short bedtime story (about 200 words) about [a character] who discovers [something surprising]. Keep it gentle and a little funny.
doneWhen: You asked for at least three changes in follow-up turns
Each change was specific (not just "make it better")
You like the final version more than the first
hints: What's one thing you'd change if this were your story?
Try: "Add a sidekick named [name] and give the ending a twist."
Worked example: turn 1 "shorter, under 120 words"; turn 2 "give the fox a catchphrase"; turn 3 "end with a question for the reader".

challenges.title: The brief that needs no questions
challenges.brief: Write one brief for a real plan (a weekend, a dinner, a trip) so complete that Claude doesn't need to ask anything you could have told it.
challenges.prompt: I'm planning [what] for [who, with ages or needs]. It matters because [why]. Budget: [amount]. Avoid [one thing]. A great result would [what success looks like]. Give me [format, like a day-by-day table]. Ask me questions first if anything is unclear.
doneWhen: Your brief says what, who, why, and what good looks like
Claude's questions (if any) were things you genuinely couldn't have known
The plan is something you'd actually use
hints: Read your brief as a stranger would. What's missing?
Add one line that starts "A great result would..."
Worked example: a 3-day trip brief with ages, a $600 budget, "no early mornings" and "table with a rainy-day backup each day".

challenges.title: Before and after
challenges.brief: Take a prompt that disappointed you this month and rewrite it using two or three examples of what you want. Compare the results side by side.
challenges.prompt:
Here are examples of the style I want:
<example>[sample 1]</example>
<example>[sample 2]</example>
<example>[sample 3]</example>
Now write [the new thing] in the same style. Match the tone and length, not the exact words.
doneWhen: You kept the old result and the new result side by side
Your examples differ from each other, so Claude copies the style, not one quirk
You can name one specific reason the new version is better
hints: Which old prompt still bugs you?
Examples beat adjectives. Instead of "punchy", show three punchy lines.
Worked example: three past newsletter intros as examples, then "write this week's intro"; the new one matched voice on the first try.

challenges.title: Same question, two settings
challenges.brief: Ask the same tricky riddle or question at two different settings (two models, or two effort levels). Which answer did you like, and why?
challenges.prompt: Here's a riddle: [your riddle]. Think it through, then give your answer and one sentence on how you got there.
doneWhen: You ran the same prompt twice with one setting changed
You noted which setting gave which answer
You wrote one sentence on why you preferred one
hints: Change only one thing at a time, or you won't know what made the difference.
Try a quick model first, then a deeper one.
Worked example: a lighter setting answered instantly and correctly; the heavier one took longer and gave the same answer. Lesson: save effort for hard jobs.

challenges.title: Is the extra effort worth it?
challenges.brief: Run one real task (a plan, an analysis, a tricky email) at a low and a high effort setting. Record time, quality and whether it was worth it.
challenges.prompt: [Your real task, described fully, with who it's for and what good looks like.]
doneWhen: You recorded roughly how long each took
You scored each result out of 10 against the same three checks
You decided which setting you'd use for this kind of job next time
hints: Pick a task where a hidden mistake would cost you something.
Write your three checks before you run it, so you don't grade on vibes.
Worked example: a trip budget at low effort missed a ferry fee; high effort caught it. Verdict: high effort for money tasks.

challenges.title: The family engine guide
challenges.brief: Make a one-page "which engine?" cheat sheet as an artifact, with three real examples per model or effort level from your own tests.
challenges.prompt: Make a one-page cheat sheet titled "Which engine?". For each setting I tested, include: what it's good at, three real examples from my tests (below), and when not to use it. Here are my results: [paste notes].
doneWhen: Every example came from a test you actually ran
Each row says when NOT to use that setting
You planted it in the garden for others
hints: Collect your notes from the Build challenge first.
Ask Claude to keep it to one page and to mark anything that's a guess.
Worked example: a three-column table (quick / everyday / deep) with real tasks in each cell.

challenges.title: Spot the fib
challenges.brief: Ask Claude to write three short facts about a topic you know well, with one made-up fact hidden among them. Find the fib, then explain how you knew.
challenges.prompt: Write three short facts about [a topic you know really well]. Make one of them subtly false, but don't tell me which. I'll try to spot it.
doneWhen: You named the false fact
You said what gave it away (a source, your own knowledge, a check)
You checked at least one of the true facts too
hints: Pick a topic where you're the expert: your town, your hobby, your job.
Look for specifics: dates, numbers and names are where errors hide.
Worked example: "The bridge opened in 1931" looked right, but the town's own website says 1937.

challenges.title: How I checked
challenges.brief: Ask Claude a real question you care about, then verify two of its claims with trusted sources. Write a one-line "how I checked" note.
challenges.prompt: [Your real question.] Please list the key claims in your answer as bullet points, say how confident you are in each, and tell me what source I could use to check it.
doneWhen: You verified two claims against sources you opened yourself
You noted any claim that turned out wrong or unclear
You wrote one line: "How I checked: ..."
hints: Ask Claude to separate facts from opinions.
Open the source; a link alone isn't a check.
Worked example: two dosage claims checked against the medicine leaflet; one matched, one needed a pharmacist.

challenges.title: The second opinion
challenges.brief: Take something you made at another bench. Open a brand-new chat, paste it in, and ask that session to critique it hard. Decide which critiques to accept.
challenges.prompt: You are reviewing work you did not write. Here it is: [paste]. List the five most important problems (accuracy, clarity, missing pieces), most serious first. For each, say how sure you are.
doneWhen: You used a fresh chat, not the one that made the work
You accepted at least one critique and rejected at least one, with a reason
You updated the original and noted what changed
hints: A fresh chat has no attachment to the first draft. That's the point.
Ask it to rank problems, so you fix what matters first.
Worked example: the reviewer caught a contradiction between slide 2 and slide 7; its tone complaint was rejected (audience is family).

challenges.title: Game-night poster
challenges.brief: Ask Claude for a one-page poster for a game night, then ask for three changes.
challenges.prompt: Make a one-page poster for a game night on [date] at [place]. Fun, readable from across a room, with the time big and a short list of games: [games].
doneWhen: The poster opened as an artifact beside the chat
You asked for three specific changes
Someone could read the date and time from across a room
hints: Specify the output: one page, what's biggest, who it's for.
Try: "Make the date twice as big and add a small trophy at the bottom."
Worked example: v1 too busy; "cut to three games and more white space" fixed it.

challenges.title: A tool you'll actually use
challenges.brief: Make a small interactive tool for your household or work: a chore wheel, a reading tracker, a packing checklist.
challenges.prompt: Build a small interactive [tool] as an artifact. It should let me [main action] and [second action]. Keep it simple, with big buttons that work on a phone. Ask me questions first if anything is unclear.
doneWhen: The tool works: you clicked through every button
Someone else used it once
You fixed at least one thing they found confusing
hints: Start with the one action you'd do daily.
Say what device it's for; phones change the design.
Worked example: a chore wheel with names, a spin button and a weekly reset.

challenges.title: Three forms, one message
challenges.brief: Make the same content as a document, a slide deck and one other form. Write which form worked best and why.
challenges.prompt: Here's my content: [paste]. Make it three ways: (1) a one-page document, (2) a five-slide deck, (3) [a third form, like a chart or a simple interactive page]. Keep the facts identical across all three.
doneWhen: All three versions say the same facts
You picked a winner and wrote two sentences on why
You planted the winner in the garden
hints: Pick content with a real audience in mind.
Ask Claude to flag any fact it changed between versions.
Worked example: the deck won for a meeting; the one-pager won for email.

challenges.title: An invitation with taste
challenges.brief: Make a birthday or event invitation by showing Claude two or three designs you like, instead of describing them.
challenges.prompt: Design an invitation for [event] on [date]. Here are examples of the look I like: [describe or attach 2 or 3]. Use [colors] and keep the text to the essentials.
doneWhen: You gave real inspiration (not just "modern")
You asked for two options and picked one
You refined it once
hints: Adjectives get generic results; examples get yours.
Ask for two options; choosing beats correcting.
Worked example: two pressed-flower invitations shown as inspiration produced a calm botanical layout.

challenges.title: Logo in three directions
challenges.brief: Ask for three different directions for a family, club or project logo. Pick one and refine it twice.
challenges.prompt: Create three distinct logo directions for [name], which is [what it is]. Direction 1: [idea]. Direction 2: [idea]. Direction 3: your best idea. Show each in color and in black and white.
doneWhen: The three directions are genuinely different
You chose one and refined it twice
It still works small and in black and white
hints: Name each direction so the options stay distinct.
Check it small: shrink it to the size of a phone icon.
Worked example: a monogram, a badge and a pictogram; the pictogram won after simplifying.

challenges.title: A tiny design system
challenges.brief: Set up a simple design system (colors, fonts, spacing, a few rules) and use it on two real pieces.
challenges.prompt: Help me write a one-page design system for [name]: 5 colors with hex values, 2 fonts, a spacing scale, and five do/don't rules. Then use it to design [piece 1] and [piece 2].
doneWhen: Your system fits on one page
Both pieces visibly follow it
You'd hand it to someone else to use
hints: Start from something you already like the look of.
Rules beat options: five clear do/don'ts.
Worked example: a family system used on a holiday card and a recipe page.

challenges.title: Chart the vote
challenges.brief: Run a quick poll (favorite pizza topping, best weekend activity) and have Claude chart the results.
challenges.prompt: Here are the votes: [list]. Make a clear bar chart, sorted from most to fewest votes, with the count on each bar and a one-line takeaway.
doneWhen: The counts on the chart match your raw votes
The chart is sorted and labeled
The takeaway is true
hints: Count a couple yourself before trusting the chart.
Ask for the raw table beside the chart.
Worked example: 11 votes, 4 for mushrooms; the chart said 5. Caught it, fixed it.

challenges.title: A sheet with real formulas
challenges.brief: Build a household budget, chore-points or reading sheet with working formulas.
challenges.prompt: Build a [type] sheet with columns for [list]. Add formulas for [totals or calculations], and explain each formula in one plain sentence.
doneWhen: The formulas calculate correctly on three rows you check by hand
You understand what each formula does
Someone else could add a row without breaking it
hints: Ask for a short explanation next to each formula.
Test with silly numbers (like 0 or 1000) to see what breaks.
Worked example: a chore-points sheet where the weekly total formula skipped Sunday until checked.

challenges.title: A dashboard you can question
challenges.brief: Build a small dashboard from your own data (or a connected app) and ask it three questions in plain English.
challenges.prompt: Here's my data: [paste or connect]. Build a small dashboard with [2 or 3 charts], show when the data was last updated, and then answer: [question 1], [question 2], [question 3].
doneWhen: Every number on it traces back to your source
The dashboard says when its data is from
You checked three answers yourself
hints: Ask Claude to show its working for each answer.
A dashboard in a doc is a snapshot. Note the date.
Worked example: monthly spending by category with a last-updated stamp; one category total was double-counted and fixed.

challenges.title: A 10-second title card
challenges.brief: Storyboard and make a short animated title card that says "Welcome to the Workshop".
challenges.prompt: Help me make a 10-second animated title card that says "Welcome to the Workshop". First write a 3-beat storyboard (what happens at 0, 3 and 7 seconds), then build it.
doneWhen: You wrote or approved a storyboard first
The text is readable the whole time
It loops or ends cleanly
hints: Beats first, build second.
Fewer moving parts look more expensive.
Worked example: beat 1 lamp glows, beat 2 title fades up, beat 3 subtitle slides in.

challenges.title: Thirty-second explainer
challenges.brief: Make a 30-second animated explainer of one idea (a rule, a process, a fun fact).
challenges.prompt: Make a 30-second animated explainer of [one idea] for [audience]. Storyboard 5 beats first with on-screen text for each, then build it. No more than 8 words on screen at once.
doneWhen: The storyboard has five beats
No screen has more than eight words
Someone who watched it can say the idea back to you
hints: One idea only. If it needs "and also", that's a second video.
Read the on-screen text aloud; if it's a mouthful, cut it.
Worked example: "How we recycle" in five beats: sort, rinse, bin, collect, done.

challenges.title: Recap reel
challenges.brief: Turn a dashboard or deck you made into a short recap video.
challenges.prompt: Turn this [deck or dashboard] into a 45-second recap video. Pick the three most important points, storyboard them, and end with one call to action.
doneWhen: You picked three points, not ten
Every figure in the video matches the source
You planted it in the garden
hints: Ask Claude which three points matter most, then decide yourself.
Check every number against the original.
Worked example: a quarterly deck became a 40-second recap with three numbers and one ask.

challenges.title: Homework Helper
challenges.brief: Make a project called Homework Helper (or Study Buddy), add one reading, and one instruction.
challenges.prompt: Project instruction: Explain things step by step, check my understanding with a question back, and never just give me the final answer to graded work.
doneWhen: You created a project with one file and one instruction
You used it in at least two chats
The instruction visibly changed how Claude answered
hints: One file and one instruction is enough to feel the difference.
Ask the same question inside and outside the project and compare.
Worked example: inside the project Claude quoted the reading and asked a check question; outside it gave a general answer.

challenges.title: The trip project
challenges.brief: Make a project for a real plan (a trip, an event, a renovation) with its key files and a "how we like plans written" instruction. Use it in three chats.
challenges.prompt: Project instruction: Plans are written as a day-by-day table with times, costs and a backup option. Keep a running list of open questions at the end. Our constraints: [list].
doneWhen: The project has the files Claude needs and nothing it doesn't
You used it in three separate chats
Each chat respected the instruction without reminders
hints: What would a helpful new teammate need to read first?
Put constraints in the instruction, not in every chat.
Worked example: itinerary, budget sheet and a packing list; three chats for lodging, food and the rainy-day plan.

challenges.title: Context audit
challenges.brief: Take an existing project. Remove anything Claude doesn't need, and test whether answers get better or worse.
challenges.prompt: Look at the files and instructions in this project. Which ones did you actually use to answer my last three questions? Which could I remove without hurting your answers?
doneWhen: You removed at least one file or instruction
You asked the same two questions before and after
You recorded whether answers got better, worse or stayed the same
hints: More context is not always better context.
Keep a copy of what you removed, just in case.
Worked example: removing an old draft fixed answers that kept quoting outdated prices.

challenges.title: Ask your calendar
challenges.brief: Connect one app you already use (like a calendar) and ask a real question about it.
challenges.prompt: Look at my calendar for this weekend. What's on, what's overlapping, and is there a free 2-hour block?
doneWhen: You connected one app you own
Claude's answer matched what's actually in the app
You know how to disconnect it
hints: Start with read-only questions.
Open the app and check Claude's answer against it.
Worked example: Claude found a clash between a game and a dinner that had gone unnoticed.

challenges.title: From note to lesson card
challenges.brief: Use a notes or docs connector to turn something you saved into something useful (a summary, a checklist, a lesson card).
challenges.prompt: Find my note called [title] and turn it into [a one-page checklist / a lesson card / a summary]. Quote the parts you used so I can check them.
doneWhen: Claude found the right note
The output quotes or links the parts it used
You checked the quotes against the original
hints: Name the note exactly, or ask Claude to list candidates first.
Ask for quotes; it makes checking fast.
Worked example: a messy video note became a five-step checklist with timestamps.

challenges.title: Chain two apps
challenges.brief: Chain two connectors so one real job flows from one app to another (an idea to a tracked task; an email to a calendar plan).
challenges.prompt: Read [source in app 1] and create [thing in app 2] from it. Before you create anything, show me exactly what you'll create and wait for my OK.
doneWhen: Claude showed you the action before taking it
The result landed in the second app correctly
You'd trust it to do the same next week, with your review
hints: Always ask to see the action first.
Pick a job you do every week.
Worked example: an idea from a notes page became a tracked issue with a checklist.

challenges.title: Make a skill by chatting
challenges.brief: Tell Claude you want to make a skill for something you do the same way every time, and let it ask you questions.
challenges.prompt: I'd like to make a skill for [a job you do the same way each time, like planning our weekly dinners]. Here's how I do it now: [your steps]. Ask me whatever you need to know about my process, then build the skill.
doneWhen: Claude asked you questions before writing the skill
You saved the skill
You used it on a real job
hints: Pick something you've explained to Claude at least twice.
Describe your real steps, including the weird ones.
Worked example: a weekly dinner skill that knows no mushrooms, Taco Tuesday and a 30-minute limit.

challenges.title: Fix it from corrections
challenges.brief: Use your skill three times. Each time it gets something wrong, correct it, then ask Claude to update the skill.
challenges.prompt: That last result missed [what]. Please update the skill so it always [the fix], and show me the change you made.
doneWhen: You used the skill three times
You updated it at least once from a correction
The next run got that thing right without reminders
hints: Corrections in chat fade; corrections in the skill stick.
Ask to see the exact change in the skill.
Worked example: the skill kept forgetting a budget cap; one update fixed it for good.

challenges.title: The Lab Lesson Writer
challenges.brief: Write a skill that turns a tip you found into a lesson card for this workshop, following its house rules.
challenges.prompt: Make a skill called lab-lesson-writer. Given a tip, it writes one lesson entry with: id, date, station, title, body (one plain paragraph), tryIt and source. Rules: plain words, one idea, only real features, and the source must be an official Anthropic page that was actually read.
doneWhen: The skill produces an entry in the right format
It refuses or flags tips it can't verify
You tested it on a tricky tip (one that's half true)
hints: Paste the house rules into the skill itself.
Test it on a tip that's out of date; it should flag it.
Worked example: it flagged a video claim about a feature name that had changed.

challenges.title: Read the rules together
challenges.brief: Open a project's CLAUDE.md (this workshop's repo will have one) and find three rules. Say why each one exists.
challenges.prompt: Here's a CLAUDE.md file: [paste]. Explain each rule in plain words and why someone might have added it.
doneWhen: You found three rules
You can say why each one exists
You spotted one rule you'd change
hints: Rules usually exist because something once went wrong.
Ask Claude which rule seems least useful.
Worked example: "never push to main" exists because pushes to main go live instantly.

challenges.title: Init and trim
challenges.brief: In Claude Code, run /init in a small folder, then trim the result to the rules that matter.
challenges.prompt: Here's the CLAUDE.md /init drafted: [paste]. Help me cut it to under 40 lines: keep the map of where things live and the rules that prevent real mistakes. Explain goals instead of shouting rules.
doneWhen: You ran /init on a real folder
The final file is shorter than the draft
Claude follows it in a fresh session
hints: A map beats an encyclopedia.
Test in a fresh session: does Claude behave as expected?
Worked example: 140 lines trimmed to 35; behavior didn't change, startup got leaner.

challenges.title: Rules that enforce house rules
challenges.brief: Write a CLAUDE.md for a content repo so that Claude follows its content rules automatically when adding entries.
challenges.prompt: Write a CLAUDE.md for this repo so that whenever you add content, you follow content/README.md: [paste rules]. Keep it short and explain why each rule matters.
doneWhen: A fresh session followed the content rules without being told
The file is under 60 lines
It contains no secrets
hints: Point to the rules file rather than copying it all.
Test with a deliberately sloppy request.
Worked example: Claude refused to add a lesson without an official source link.

challenges.title: Your own colors
challenges.brief: Ask Claude Code to make a custom theme in your favorite colors.
challenges.prompt: Make me a Claude Code theme in [colors] with a calm, readable look. Explain how to switch it on and off.
doneWhen: The theme works
You know how to switch it off
It's still easy to read
hints: Start with two colors you love.
Check contrast: can you read it in daylight?
Worked example: a forest-green and brass theme, switched on in a minute.

challenges.title: One mod, one week
challenges.brief: Add one mod you think will help, and keep a simple note for a week: did it help?
challenges.prompt: I'm adding [mod]. Before I do, explain in plain words what it can see and change on my computer.
doneWhen: You read what the mod can access before installing
You kept a note for a week
You decided to keep it or remove it
hints: If you can't explain what it does, don't install it.
Removing a mod is as much a skill as adding one.
Worked example: a usage panel kept; a noisy notifier removed after two days.

challenges.title: Build a celebration mod
challenges.brief: Describe and build a small mod that celebrates when something good happens (a merged change, a finished task).
challenges.prompt: Build a small Claude Code mod that [celebrates when X happens]. Keep it tiny and explain every permission it needs.
doneWhen: The mod works on a real event
It asks for no more permissions than it needs
You'd be comfortable sharing it with family
hints: Smallest version first.
List the permissions before writing code.
Worked example: a confetti line in the status bar when a pull request merges.

challenges.title: Draw your helper
challenges.brief: Watch the Director's notes and sketch (or list) what your own helper would do each morning, and what it should never do without asking.
challenges.prompt: Help me write a one-page "morning helper" plan: five things it checks each morning, three things it can draft for me, and five things it must never do without my yes.
doneWhen: You listed five morning checks
You listed what it must never do without asking
Someone else read it and understood it
hints: Start with your most annoying weekly task.
The "never without asking" list matters most.
Worked example: checks school dates and bills; never sends, pays or deletes without a yes.

challenges.title: A logistics channel
challenges.brief: Set up one channel for a real area of life (school dates, practice schedules, a project) with clear goals and ground rules. Review its first three briefs.
challenges.prompt: Here are my goals for this channel: [goals]. Ground rules: [rules]. Before you take any action, tell me what you plan to do.
doneWhen: You wrote goals and ground rules first
You reviewed the first three briefs
You corrected it at least once and it remembered
hints: Goals plus ground rules beat clever prompts.
Correct it in plain words: "from now on, ..."
Worked example: a sports channel that drafts carpool messages but never sends them.

challenges.title: Weekly what's new
challenges.brief: Pair your assistant with a weekly routine that produces a short "what's new" summary for your family or team.
challenges.prompt: Every [day] at [time], summarize what changed this week in [area], in five bullets, with links to where each came from. Flag anything that needs a decision.
doneWhen: It ran on schedule at least once
Every bullet links to its source
You checked two bullets against their sources
hints: Ask for sources on every bullet.
Check the first few runs closely; trust grows from checks.
Worked example: a Monday summary of the workshop's new cards, with links.
